groups.title: Get started
groups.summary: Install Tachyon, build your first app, learn where each file goes, and preview it.

groups.title: Pages (Tac)
groups.summary: Tac is the frontend part of Tachyon. Make pages, show values, and keep data in the browser.

groups.title: Server (Yon)
groups.summary: Yon is the backend part of Tachyon. Answer requests, return models, check values, and read settings and data.

groups.title: Real-time
groups.summary: Send messages while a page is open: streams, sockets and topics.

groups.title: Languages
groups.summary: Choose the language of each service and controller.

groups.title: Apps on devices
groups.summary: Build the same pages as a desktop or mobile app.

groups.title: Going further
groups.summary: Topics for later: injection, behavior annotations, middleware, other languages, modules, security, cohesive services, utilities, helpers the design rules and simpler forms.

groups.title: Operations
groups.summary: Test, build, deploy and follow requests in the logs.

groups.title: Cookbook
groups.summary: Examples for real applications that use Tac (the frontend) and Yon (the backend) together.

groups.title: Reference
groups.summary: Look up an annotation, a routing name, an error code or a word.

install.title: Install
install.summary: Tachyon is a full-stack framework: it makes both the frontend (the pages that run in the browser) and the backend (the server that answers requests). Tac is the frontend part. Yon is the backend part. You install one program, `ty`. It creates, previews, builds and tests your app.

first-app.title: Your first app
first-app.summary: Build a small app in five steps. First make a page. Then add a service with a field that updates the page. Then add a Yon controller that returns a model, and call the controller from the page. Last, test the service and the controller. Each step shows every file, where it goes, and what you see.

project-folders.title: Project folders and roles
project-folders.summary: Tachyon finds your code by its folder and its file name, so you write no setup code. A role is the job of a class, such as service or controller. The role decides the folder. A file in the wrong folder fails with `TY1310` before the app runs. Role types for `Allow`, such as `Admin`, are empty classes in `server/roles`.

preview-and-build.title: Preview and build
preview-and-build.summary: `ty preview` runs your app while you work, and it builds the app again when you save a file. `ty bundle` builds the files that you publish. `ty start` serves those files.

pages.title: Pages and URLs
pages.summary: Each folder under `client/pages` is one part of a URL. The `tac.html` file in a folder is the page for that URL. A folder whose name starts with `_`, such as `_topic`, matches any value in that part of the URL.

templates.title: Templates
templates.summary: A template is the `tac.html` file of a page or a component. It is HTML with a few additions. Braces show values. `on:` attributes run a method when an event happens. The `loop`, `logic` and `switch` elements repeat or hide parts of the page. A component is a part of a page that you can use again.

services.title: Services
services.summary: A service is a class in `client/services` that holds the data and the actions of a view. The view names the service, and Tachyon creates it. For example, a view refers to `BasketService` as `basket` and shows `{basket.count}`. When a field changes, the page updates.

browser-storage.title: Saving data in the browser
browser-storage.summary: A service can keep data in the browser. A field marked `@LocalState` or `@SessionState` keeps its value after a reload. A browser Store keeps records, and a cache keeps answers so that the page does not ask for them again.

application-events.title: Events between services
application-events.summary: An event is a message that one service publishes and other services receive. The publisher does not need to know who listens. This page also shows the start and stop methods of a service (lifecycle hooks), in the browser and on the server.

web-components.title: Components in other apps
web-components.summary: A component can leave your Tac app. List it in `tac.elements`, and the build makes it a custom element: a standard HTML tag that a plain HTML page, React, Angular, Vue or another Tac app can use. Values go in as attributes or properties, events come out as DOM events, and the children of the tag show in its slots. Each element comes with TypeScript declarations, and a project can export elements without having a page.

controllers.title: Controllers
controllers.summary: A controller is a class in `server/controllers` that answers HTTP requests. Each method with a route annotation, such as `GetRoute`, answers one kind of request on one path. An argument marked `FromPath`, `FromQuery` or `FromBody` gets its value from the request. Every route also says who may call it with `Public`, `SignedIn` or `Allow(Role)`; the build stops without it.

models.title: Models and JSON answers
models.summary: A model is a data type in `server/models`. A controller method takes models and returns them. Yon turns the value that a method returns into a JSON answer.

checking-values.title: Checking values
checking-values.summary: Yon checks the values that a caller sends before your method runs. A wrong value gets an error answer, and your method never sees it.

error-handlers.title: Error handlers
error-handlers.summary: An error handler turns an error that your code throws into a clear answer for the caller. You write it once, and it works for every controller of its language.

route-access.title: Who may call a route
route-access.summary: Every route says who may call it: anyone, any signed-in user, or only some roles. One identity provider class tells Tachyon who is signed in, and Tachyon answers 401 or 403 before your code runs.

application-configuration.title: Settings and configuration
application-configuration.summary: Server settings live in `server/application.json`. Page settings live in `client/manifest.json`. Secrets, such as passwords, live in `.env` and never reach the browser. A class marked `Settings` gets its field values from these files.

calling-the-server.title: Calling the server from a page
calling-the-server.summary: A page gets data from the server through a client class. Mark the class with `HTTPClient` and its methods with `GetRequest`, `PostRequest` and the other request annotations. A service gets the client with `Needs` and calls its methods. In JavaScript, TypeScript, Dart, C#, F#, Rust, Go, Kotlin, Swift, Java and Ruby, a client whose Setup gives it no adapter sends its request through the browser to the server of the page, without cookies. A C++ client has no Setup, so it always uses this transport. This browser transport refuses every other origin. Lua cannot use `HTTPClient` (`TY1308`). A request to another host goes through a Setup adapter, and that host must be listed in `tac.outgoing.hosts`.

server-data.title: Server data
server-data.summary: Yon can connect to a SQL database, to the FYLO document store and to Redis for you. You name them in `server/application.json`, and a Store class gets them with `Needs`. Values always go in as parameters: Tachyon refuses query text built from pieces. With FYLO, DataSource also reads and changes documents by id, scrolls through any number of them with a cursor, manages collections and runs a durable queue.

streams.title: Streams
streams.summary: A stream keeps one HTTP answer open and sends many messages on it. On the server, mark the method with `StreamRoute`. In the page, a client method marked `StreamRequest` receives the messages. A stream route says who may call it like any other route.

sockets.title: Sockets
sockets.summary: A socket (a WebSocket) is a connection that stays open, so the browser and the server can both send messages at any time. On the server, mark a controller with `SocketRoute`. In the page, a client method marked `SocketRequest` connects to it. The socket class also says who may connect: `Public`, `SignedIn` or `Allow(Role)` on the class.

topics.title: Topics
topics.summary: A topic is a model marked `Topic`. When one part of the app publishes a value of that model, Tachyon sends it to the listeners in the Yon languages that have topics and in open pages.

service-languages.title: Choosing a service language
service-languages.summary: You can write a Tac service in JavaScript, TypeScript, Rust, Go, C#, F#, Swift, Kotlin, Java, Dart or Ruby. Lua, Python and C++ work with limits. "Which languages can I use?" lists every language, what it can do, and the languages that Tachyon does not support. A service runs in the page on every target, also inside a native app. Some native hosts link Rust, Swift, Kotlin or C# services instead.

yon-languages.title: The Yon languages
yon-languages.summary: Yon runs controllers written in JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, Groovy, Kotlin, C#, F#, PHP, Rust, Dart, Go, Ruby and Lua. Every language uses the same annotations and the same folders.

native-services.title: Rust, Go and C# in the browser
native-services.summary: A service written in Rust, Go, C#, F#, Swift, Kotlin, Java, Dart or Ruby can run in the browser as WebAssembly, a compiled format that browsers run. Lua and Python services run there too, on runtimes that Tachyon ships, and C++ services that Emscripten compiles, all with limits. In a desktop or mobile app, Swift, Kotlin, C# and Rust services can run as native code instead.

devices.title: Targets
devices.summary: A target is the kind of app that you build: web, macos, windows, linux, ios or android. You write the pages once. The web target runs in a browser. The other targets put the same pages in a desktop or mobile app.

native-hosts.title: Native hosts
native-hosts.summary: A native host is the desktop or mobile app that Tachyon builds for a target. It shows your pages in the WebView, the browser view that is built into the operating system. So the app shows exactly what the browser shows.

platform-apis.title: Platform APIs
platform-apis.summary: A platform API is a feature of the device, such as the tray or the file system. In a native host, the page is the same as in the browser. A service that is compiled for the platform uses the platform API directly.

window-controls.title: Window controls
window-controls.summary: In a desktop or mobile app, `client/manifest.json` describes the window that the app opens. It lists the window controls that a page may ask for; by default, a page may ask for none. On macOS, it can also let the page reach the top edge of the window, with an integrated title bar.

native-menus.title: Native menus
native-menus.summary: A macOS, Linux or Windows app that Tachyon builds has a menu bar. `tac.application.menus` in `client/manifest.json` adds your own items to the File, View and Help menus. An item opens a page of the app, or it runs a menu action: a method of a service that lives as long as the app.

dependency-injection.title: Dependency injection
dependency-injection.summary: Dependency injection means that Tachyon creates the objects that a class needs and puts them into its fields. Mark a field with `Needs`, or mark the class with `NeedsAll`. `Lifetime` says how long one object lives.

behavior-annotations.title: Behavior annotations
behavior-annotations.summary: Behavior annotations add common work to a method without extra code, such as caching, retries, value checks, stores and settings. The same annotations work in Tac and in Yon, in every service language except Lua in Tac, where the build refuses them. A Python Tac service writes each method that has one of them with `async def`.

middleware.title: Middleware
middleware.summary: Middleware is code that runs before every request and after every response. Put it in a `middleware.<ext>` file at the project root. Who may call a route is not middleware work: routes say it with `Public`, `SignedIn` or `Allow(Role)`.

relays-and-gateways.title: Relays and gateways
relays-and-gateways.summary: A gateway lets a method in one language call a class that is written in another language. A relay sends a request to a program that Yon does not run itself.

modules-and-lifecycle.title: Modules and lifecycle
modules-and-lifecycle.summary: This page explains how Tachyon groups your files into programs, and how it starts and stops the process that answers a request.

isolation-and-security.title: Isolation and security
isolation-and-security.summary: Tachyon refuses four dangerous mistakes when it builds, runs each request in its own process, and adds security headers to every answer. This page explains these rules and limits, and the rules for code that runs in the browser.

cohesive-services.title: Cohesive services
cohesive-services.summary: A public method of a service or a controller only coordinates. Each private method holds at most one decision or one loop. The build checks this with TY1314.

utilities.title: Utilities
utilities.summary: Tachyon refuses a block of code that repeats (TY1315). Move it into a static method of a utility class in client/shared/utils (Tac) or server/utils (Yon), and call it from both places.

helpers.title: Helpers, utilities and private methods
helpers.summary: One question decides where shared code goes: a helper when it needs other classes, saved state, lifecycle hooks or a Fake in tests; otherwise a utility, a private method or a service.

dependency-direction.title: Dependencies point down
dependency-direction.summary: A class needs only the classes below it, and no chain of classes loops back. The build checks this with TY1327.

plain-english-names.title: Plain-English names
plain-english-names.summary: Every word of a class, method, field or parameter name is an English word, a short technical word or a word of your domain. The build checks this with TY1328.

small-signatures.title: Small signatures
small-signatures.summary: A method takes at most four parameters, and a class needs at most five other classes. The build checks this with TY1329.

named-values.title: Named values
named-values.summary: A text or number used twice, or a number in a condition, gets a name: a class constant. The build checks this with TY1330.

public-only-when-used.title: Public only when used
public-only-when-used.summary: A method or field of a class is public only when a view, another class or Tachyon uses it. Everything else is private. The build checks this with TY1333.

types-in-every-language.title: Types in every language
types-in-every-language.summary: Every field, parameter and return value of a class states its type: a type comment where the language has no type syntax, the native type where it has one. The build checks this with TY1356.

simpler-forms.title: Simpler forms
simpler-forms.summary: When a piece of code has a simpler form that reads more plainly, `ty preview` and `ty test` suggest it with codes TY1340 to TY1355. A suggestion never stops the build, and `ty migrate fix --write` applies it.

test-units.title: Test units
test-units.summary: A test unit is a class in `server/tests` or `client/tests` whose name ends with `Test`. `ty test` finds and runs every test unit. `ty preview` does not start while a public method of an annotated class has no test.

build-and-deploy.title: Build and deploy
build-and-deploy.summary: `ty bundle` builds the files that you publish, and `ty start` serves them. This page shows the options for a release.

webassembly-compilers.title: WebAssembly compilers per language
webassembly-compilers.summary: A release build compiles each WebAssembly service language with the compiler and settings that give the smallest download. This page shows which compiler each language uses, why, and what it costs.

request-ids.title: Request IDs and error reports
request-ids.summary: Every request has an ID that links its log lines. When something fails, the error report has a stable code, so you can find what happened.

cookbook.title: Cookbook
cookbook.summary: Practical recipes for building Tachyon apps with a frontend-first workflow (you build the client first). Most recipes need only client/. When a recipe needs a server, it shows the smallest controller that answers it.

annotations.title: Annotations A–Z
annotations.summary: An annotation is a marker that you put on a class, a field or a method. It tells Tachyon what to do. This page first lists every annotation from A to Z with one line about what it does. Then each group of annotations has a working example in every language that accepts it. Tac is the frontend realm (one side of the app), and Yon is the backend realm. When a realm or a language does not accept an annotation, the section says so and explains why.

routing-annotations.title: Routing glossary
routing-annotations.summary: Routes answer incoming requests. Clients send outgoing requests. These names explain where paths and argument values come from. Access annotations say who may call a route.

error-codes.title: Error codes
error-codes.summary: Every error from `ty` has a stable code, such as `TY1310`. The code stays the same when the message text changes, so you can search for it. This page lists every code, and the codes that a running page can get.

glossary.title: Glossary
glossary.summary: Short meanings of the words that the guides use.
